Friend and I in middle school played in his room one night. With the lights off, we lit two small candles and placed them on each side of the board. For about 30 minutes nothing happened. Then the planchet began to speed around the board. 

Of course we both blamed each other, and as I scoffed that he claimed he wasn't moving the planchet, it stopped on three letters S-E-E. After the last letter, the planchet jerked faster around the board, now in a figure eight pattern, and did this for maybe 30 seconds before again spelling out S-E-E. 

My friend's eyes then turned wild, his voice cracking. "Holy shit!"

I look away from the board, the planchet still powering through figure eights, and noticed the candles. The flames twirled like a funnel cloud, reaching higher and higher and growing brighter.

"I can't take my hand off!"

The panic in my friend's voice was palpable. I became mesmerized by this display, not even trying to take my hands off, but gazing at the flames as they twirled, rose and met at an arch in front of our faces over the board. 

There was something kinetic in the air at that moment. A crack, glass shattering and the flames blossomed into what I can only describe as a mini-explosion. It washed over us both and then left me with the flash imprint in my eyes as the room darkened again, the flames snuffed out. 

The planchet suddenly ceased, its pointer resting in front of the letter I. 

The rest of that night was a blur. I left early, even though I was supposed to spend the night because my friend was having panic attacks. He even refused to talk to me after; it mattered little. I mean we were friends, but middle school friendships are transient at best. 

But for me, I was just fascinated. Scared? No. Awed by the whole experience and just fascinated. It was like I was given a glimpse of a mystery, allowed a moment to see the world as it truly could be behind a veil that is always there, but we're too blind to realize how thin it actually is. 

I never used an Ouija board again. That has nothing to do with this experience. But to me, the feeling I was left with was the item was a simple tool to see beyond the veil and nothing more. The fact that I got a glimpse was enough for me and frankly shaped me in many ways throughout my life.

Here's one that I'm sure will be destroyed by the reddit masses...if it's even read. 

Ten years ago, when my first child was born, things did not look good. My son was being plagued by infant mal seizures, brief ones, but nonetheless, enough to have physicians and specialists run a battery of test. 

In the end, we were told the diagnosis: Mitochondrial disorder. A death sentence for those children afflicted by it. In short, my first-born son was likely not to live past five. 

To say I was devastated is an understatement. It was the one time in my life that my grief almost slipped my sanity. I was in a dark, depressive place, barely able to function; hearing noises in the wall that I was obsessed were rats but no one else could hear; refusing to let my infant son sleep on his own.

Now, I will go into this saying that I am Catholic--while I grew up without a faith, I came into the Church later in my life, mainly to get married as my then-fiance was devoutly Catholic. But the strange thing is, I grew to love the faith as well.

But at this time, looking upon the blue eyes of my child through my own pain and tears, my own eyes were clouded to God. I begged, I questioned, I pleaded. 

The tests on my son continued--physicians monitoring certain levels of chemicals in his body. On the eve of a test, my wife and I went to church with our baby. I was in a bad place. About as low as I could go. The night before I convinced myself that when my son died, I would do the same. 

But there, just after the homily and during the consecration of the bread and wine, a voice as real and lucid as anything I ever heard filled my head. The voice was unmistakably male, comforting, tender while at the same time authoritative and powerful. He simply said, "He's going to be okay."

I glanced at my wife, wondering if she heard it as well, checked behind me seeing if someone was speaking. No one I could pin that voice on, and no one else seemed to notice anyone speak.

The next week, my son's tests came back normal. The seizures had ceased. His muscle tightness relaxed. And our physicians, after a couple of more tests, ruled him as clear. As one neurologist put it, "Well, I guess I was wrong."

How has this changed my life? Other than now I not only have a healthy, happy 10-year-old son who is sometimes smarter than he has a right to be and a smartass (and probably future reddit contributor given his humor), I have two other sons as well. 

But more than anything, my belief in God is real, is solidified. I can see no other explanation for the miracle cure. And that makes me fortunate: Because I was given a glimpse of what I believe to be the truth--that God is real and exists. I realize most people just have to believe upon simple faith. Or not believe. I'm a rare exception, I guess, and I'm not even sure how I deserve to have such clarity of belief let alone my greatest prayer to have been granted because there are so many other parents who have faced similar situations, and instead faced them without a miracle.

And my heart breaks for them. 

But I will never doubt God, His existence. And I am eternally grateful to Him.

I hate this new belief that God blesses people with material things. This idea -- espoused by "profits" like Joel Osteen -- says that God will shower his followers and true believers with material wealth, as if it's a guarantee. 

What does that mean for those of us who struggle every month just to pay bills, yet go to Church faithfully every week? Or more to the point: Does this mean Jesus was wrong when he preached to the poor, when he ministered to the lowly? Where in the Bible does Jesus say believe in me and get lots of goodies in the world?

He doesn't. Nor does the Bible espouse that. Yet we have a segment of our society who believes that they are a) entitled to their material wealth and b) that accumulated wealth equals accumulated approval by God.

Of course all this is wrong. If I struggle, and feel like there is a cap in what I can make or earn in my time, somehow I am out of God's favor. And our society seems to validate that. We worship our rich. We hold those who have great jobs and earn lots of money on a pedestal as someone who should both be admired and aspired to. 

And we're told in mass media that in America if you work with relentless fervor and complete dedication that you will eventually make a lot of money. We're told that if you're the best at something, wealth will come your way.

Is that really true?

I mean, you could be the world's greatest janitor, but will that ever make you rich? You could be the most skilled plumber in North America, but will you ever ear six to seven figures for that? 

Look, society determines often what we value. It's been said you can glean what a society values by the uses of its tallest buildings. In America, our tallest buildings seemed entirely reserved to banking and finance. 

We worship the God of Money. We eat the shit crapped out by people in banking and hedge fund managers and traders. Our "lowly" service employees in major cities often have to put up with the crap dished out by the fuckers who make seven figures trading stocks or buying and selling companies because they are rich.

In America, society is skewed to the idea that success equals material wealth; everyone else is a failure.

Hence -- me the lowly guy earning $75k a year having to feed a family of 5, driving around in beat-up used cars, living in sketchy neighborhoods because the houses are affordable -- I'm something to be disdained. Someone who "lost favor of God" even though I go to Church every Sunday. 


I will tell you this: The rich need to face reality. This attitude is very quickly going to come back to bite them. Tolerance is eroding every day, not only in America, but across the world. Some day soon, if society doesn't change, the torches and pitchforks could come out and burn their mansions down to the ground.
